Neonates of the desert tortoise emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs after a developmental period of approximately 118 days [ab = approximately 118 days] when eggs are incubated at a constant 30 °C [T = 30 °C]. At the moment of eclosion, hatchlings possess a mean plastron length of 4.7 centimeters [Lb = 4.7 centimeters], a dimension that reflects the constraints imposed by the calcareous eggshell. The wet weight at birth is similarly modest, averaging 27.5 grams [Wwb = 27.5 grams], a value consistent with the energetic demands of the prolonged incubation typical of this species. These morphological traits at hatching set the stage for the subsequent growth trajectory, which is characterized by a slow but steady increase in body size over the first several years of life. The transition from the lecithotrophic larval stage to the onset of exogenous feeding occurs shortly after emergence, as the young tortoises begin to consume herbaceous vegetation and succulents available in their arid environment, marking a critical nutritional shift that influences both survival and future growth rates.

A comprehensive understanding of the sexual maturation process in the desert tortoise requires consideration of both size-based and age-based thresholds. In females, the onset of puberty occurs when the plastron length reaches approximately 17.9 centimeters [Lp = approximately 17.9 centimeters], whereas in males a slightly larger plastron length of 18.2 centimeters [Lp = 18.2 centimeters] signals the attainment of reproductive maturity. The time since birth at which this developmental milestone is achieved has been estimated at 5,500 days [tp = 5,500 days] for both sexes under the thermal conditions typical of their natural habitat, specifically at 24 °C [T = 24 °C]. This delay of roughly fifteen years is a hallmark of a slow life history strategy, which is further reflected in the substantial body masses associated with the pubertal transition. Females typically weigh approximately 1,229 grams [Wwp = approximately 1,229 grams] at this juncture, while males achieve a wet weight at puberty of about 1,292 grams [Wwp = about 1,292 grams], underscoring the considerable somatic investment required before reproduction can commence.

Sexual dimorphism in body size becomes most apparent when examining the ultimate dimensions achieved by fully mature adults. The asymptote of female growth is reached at a plastron length of 22.6 centimeters [Li = 22.6 centimeters], a value that, when combined with the length-weight relationship derived from congeneric species, corresponds to an ultimate wet weight of 2,473 grams [Wwi = 2,473 grams]. In contrast, males attain a larger terminal size, with the maximum plastron length reaching 26.0 centimeters [Li = 26.0 centimeters] and an associated adult body mass of 3,765 grams [Wwi = 3,765 grams]. This pronounced male-biased sexual size dimorphism is relatively unusual among chelonians and is thought to be linked to intrasexual competition for mates, as larger males may possess advantages in agonistic encounters. The attainment of these maximal sizes demands decades of consistent growth, with the dietary quality of the Mojave Desert’s ephemeral vegetation playing a crucial role in determining whether individuals approach these theoretical upper boundaries.

Reproductive output in this species is constrained by both environmental conditions and the considerable energy demands of egg production. Under the thermal regime characteristic of active metabolic periods in Gopherus agassizii, which is approximately 24 °C [T = 24 °C], the maximum reproductive rate is achieved through a combination of moderate clutch sizes and limited annual breeding frequency. Field studies indicate that females typically produce one egg per clutch [N_R_i = one egg per clutch] and approximately 8 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 8 clutches per year]. This annual reproductive output is modest compared to many other Testudinidae, reflecting the high per-offspring investment and the risks of egg desiccation in the xeric environment. The timing of the first egg clutch is closely tied to the onset of the summer monsoon season, which provides the moisture necessary for successful embryonic development within the subterranean nest chamber.

Longevity represents one of the most remarkable life-history traits of the desert tortoise, with individuals capable of surviving for many decades in their native habitat. The maximum recorded lifespan at a mean annual temperature of 24 °C [T = 24 °C] has been documented at approximately 22,922 days [am = approximately 22,922 days], a figure that is consistent with the age estimates from skeletal annuli and long-term mark-recapture studies. This exceptional longevity is matched by an equally extended period of reproductive activity, as sexually mature adults can continue breeding for several decades after reaching the pubertal threshold of 5,500 days since birth [tp = 5,500 days since birth] when maintained at 24 °C [T = 24 °C]. The evolution of such a slow-paced life cycle is closely tied to the unpredictability of food resources in the Mojave and Sonoran deserts, where favorable reproductive years are intermittent. In comparison to other North American chelonians, the desert tortoise exhibits one of the highest survival rates among adults, a demographic trait that offsets the relatively low annual fecundity and protracted period of growth before maturity.
